title_en: Jacques-Louis David, The Death of Socrates, 1787
title_el: Ζακ-Λουί Νταβίντ, Ο θάνατος του Σωκράτη, 1787
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (31.45)
licence: CC0 1.0 (Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access)
why: Socrates (socrates) is in the first talk on the path; Athena tells his calm death (socrates-death) as philosophy's practice of dying (meletethanatou, Phaedo 64a on the bookshelf).

title_en: Votive relief from Mantineia, perhaps Diotima, 420–410 BC
title_el: Αναθηματικό ανάγλυφο από τη Μαντίνεια, ίσως η Διοτίμα, 420–410 π.Χ.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photograph); the relief itself is public domain
attribution: Yair Haklai, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Diotima (diotima, weight 5, first talk) teaches Socrates the ladder of eros that Nostos uses for progress; this seer from Mantineia, Diotima's city, is traditionally taken to be Diotima, which is not certain.

title_en: Achilles Painter, A Muse playing the lyre on Mount Helicon, white-ground lekythos, 440–430 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος του Αχιλλέα, Μούσα που παίζει λύρα στον Ελικώνα, λευκή λήκυθος, 440–430 π.Χ.
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Bibi Saint-Pol: PD-self)
why: Music and the Muses (music, weight 5) come up in the first talk; for Athena music is Apollo's fourth power, the art of harmonising opposites.

title_en: Exekias, Dionysus sailing among dolphins, Attic black-figure kylix, c. 530 BC
title_el: Εξηκίας, Ο Διόνυσος ταξιδεύει ανάμεσα σε δελφίνια, αττική μελανόμορφη κύλικα, περ. 530 π.Χ.
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Bibi Saint-Pol: PD-self)
why: Dionysus (dionysus) comes up in the first talk on the path: Athena reads him as the god incarnate who leads festivals and plays (myth apollodionysus), and returns to him with the Titans and the mirror.

title_en: The so-called Hestia Giustiniani, Roman copy (117–138 AD) of a Greek original of c. 470–460 BC
title_el: Η λεγόμενη Εστία Τζουστινιάνι, ρωμαϊκό αντίγραφο (117–138 μ.Χ.) ελληνικού πρωτοτύπου του περ. 470–460 π.Χ.
date: 117–138 AD, after an original of c. 470–460 BC
licence: CC BY 4.0 (photograph); the statue itself is public domain
attribution: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Hestia (hestia, first talk) is for Athena the one god who never leaves the centre, the sacred fire at the centre of the heart (myths hestia_olympus, hestialamp). "So-called": the statue is only traditionally named Hestia.

title_en: The Nativity, mosaic in the Daphni Monastery, late 11th century
title_el: Η Γέννηση του Χριστού, ψηφιδωτό της Μονής Δαφνίου, τέλη 11ου αι.
licence: CC BY 4.0 (photograph); the mosaic itself is public domain
attribution: Jacob Freeland, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Athena decodes the Nativity (christianity; myth nativity): the child born in a cave, laid in a manger with two animals by it. This Greek mosaic near Athens shows the cave.

images: Life as a theatre, each person an actor
Life as a video game or living dream; Dionysian theatre
title_en: The Theatre of Dionysus on the south slope of the Acropolis, photograph by Jebulon, 2015
title_el: Το θέατρο του Διονύσου στη νότια κλιτύ της Ακρόπολης, φωτογραφία του Jebulon, 2015
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer; tourists removed by retouching)
why: Athena reads life as Dionysus' theatre: each of us is given a role, a costume and a name, and the spectator wakes to the spectacle (myth theatre; divineplay).

title_en: Zeus or Poseidon, bronze from Cape Artemision, c. 460 BC
title_el: Ο Δίας ή ο Ποσειδώνας του Αρτεμισίου, χάλκινο άγαλμα, περ. 460 π.Χ.
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer, Jebulon)
why: Zeus (zeus) is in the first talk on the path and Poseidon has his trident (myth poseidontrident); scholars still disagree which god this is, which is why it is offered for both.

images: The soul as a lyre Apollo plays; virtues as notes
title_en: Apollo with his kithara pours a libation, white-ground kylix from Delphi, 480–470 BC
title_el: Ο Απόλλων σπένδει κρατώντας την κιθάρα του, λευκή κύλικα από τους Δελφούς, 480–470 π.Χ.
artist: Attributed to the Pistoxenos Painter (or the Berlin Painter, or Onesimos)
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photograph); the vase itself is public domain
attribution: Zde, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Apollo (apollo, weight 5) is Delphi's god and the subject of Athena's five steps of awakening; Athena calls the soul a lyre Apollo plays. Found at Delphi itself.

title_en: Plato, Roman copy of the portrait by Silanion (c. 370 BC)
title_el: Ο Πλάτων, ρωμαϊκό αντίγραφο του πορτρέτου του Σιλανίωνα (περ. 370 π.Χ.)
date: Roman copy of an original of c. 370 BC
licence: CC BY 2.5 (photograph); the bust itself is public domain
attribution: © Marie-Lan Nguyen / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5/)
why: Plato (plato, weight 5) is the thinker Athena returns to most; the portrait type was made for his Academy in Athens.

title_en: Head thought to be Plotinus, from Ostia, 3rd century AD
title_el: Κεφαλή που θεωρείται ότι εικονίζει τον Πλωτίνο, από την Όστια, 3ος αι. μ.Χ.
licence: CC BY 3.0 (photograph); the head itself is public domain
attribution: Sailko, CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Plotinus (plotinus, weight 5) is Athena's guide to the One and the flight "to the dear fatherland" (Ennead I.6.8 on the bookshelf). The Commons page itself says the identification is plausible but not proven.

title_en: Raphael, The School of Athens, 1509–1511
title_el: Ραφαήλ, Η Σχολή των Αθηνών, 1509–1511
licence: Public domain (PD-Art)
why: Philosophy (philosophy) is the third most frequent idea in Athena's teaching; the fresco gathers the Greek thinkers around Plato and Aristotle.

title_en: After Hans Weiditz, Gyges finds the ring in a bronze horse, woodcut from a German Cicero, Augsburg, 1531
title_el: Κατά σχέδιο του Χανς Βάιντιτς, Ο Γύγης βρίσκει το δαχτυλίδι μέσα σε χάλκινο άλογο, ξυλογραφία από γερμανική έκδοση του Κικέρωνα, Άουγκσμπουργκ, 1531
artist: Anonymous woodcutter after a design by Hans Weiditz (II); published by Heinrich Steiner
licence: CC0 1.0 (Rijksmuseum)
why: Athena tells the Ring of Gyges as power without limits that cannot last (myth gyges), next to Athena's reading of justice as balance held from the middle (justice).

title_en: Workshop of Hendrick Goltzius, Apollo kills the Python, engraving, 1589
title_el: Εργαστήριο του Χέντρικ Χόλτσιους, Ο Απόλλων σκοτώνει τον Πύθωνα, χαλκογραφία, 1589
artist: Workshop of Hendrick Goltzius, after his design; verses by Franco Estius
licence: CC0 1.0 (Rijksmuseum)
why: Apollo slays the Python to found Delphi, which Athena reads as the power that dissolves what is rotten and stagnant in us: "we are the oracle of Delphi" (myths python, python-slaying; apollo, delphi, katharsis).

images: Delphi's entrance as a riddle instead of a welcome
title_en: The Temple of Apollo at Delphi (4th century BC), photograph by Jebulon, 2018
title_el: Ο ναός του Απόλλωνα στους Δελφούς (4ος αι. π.Χ.), φωτογραφία του Jebulon, 2018
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer)
why: "Know thyself" was inscribed at this temple; Athena reads the Delphic inscriptions and the E as a riddle at the entrance (knowthyself, delphice; myths delphicinscriptions, apollo_delphi).

title_en: A Karagiozis shadow puppet, Athens, photograph by Aeleftherios, 2008
title_el: Φιγούρα του Καραγκιόζη από το θέατρο σκιών, Αθήνα, φωτογραφία του Aeleftherios, 2008
licence: CC BY-SA 3.0, or GFDL, at the reuser's choice
attribution: Aeleftherios, CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Athena compares the play of shadows to Karagiozis: the awakened watch the shadow play while remembering "I am not this" (divineplay; myth karagiozis).

title_en: Annibale Carracci, The Choice of Heracles, 1596
title_el: Αννίμπαλε Καράτσι, Η επιλογή του Ηρακλή, 1596
licence: Public domain (PD-Art)
why: Athena uses Heracles at the fork between Virtue and Vice: like him, we choose ἀρετή or vice at every moment (arete, noandyes; myth heracles-crossroads).

title_en: Penelope Painter, Odysseus kills the suitors, Attic red-figure skyphos, c. 440 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος της Πηνελόπης, Ο Οδυσσέας σκοτώνει τους μνηστήρες, αττικός ερυθρόμορφος σκύφος, περ. 440 π.Χ.
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer, Gary Todd, on Flickr; Flickr review passed)
why: For Athena, clearing the suitors from Ithaca takes longer than the voyage home (odyssey-suitors; Odyssey 22 on the bookshelf): the inner work after the return.

title_en: Pythagoras with bells, glasses, a monochord and pipes, woodcut from Franchino Gaffurio's Theorica musicae, 1492
title_el: Ο Πυθαγόρας με καμπάνες, ποτήρια, μονόχορδο και αυλούς, ξυλογραφία από το Theorica musicae του Φρανκίνο Γκαφούριο, 1492
artist: Unknown woodcutter, published by Franchino Gaffurio
licence: Public domain (PD-old-100)
why: Pythagoras (pythagoras, weight 5) gets a whole study cycle from Athena, and harmony (harmony) as number and music runs through it; this is the classic image of Pythagoras finding the ratios of harmony.

title_en: Eros stringing his bow, Roman copy after a bronze by Lysippos (338–335 BC)
title_el: Ο Έρως τεντώνει το τόξο του, ρωμαϊκό αντίγραφο χάλκινου έργου του Λυσίππου (338–335 π.Χ.)
date: Roman copy of an original of 338–335 BC
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer, Daderot)
why: Eros (eros, weight 5) is for Athena a path of awakening and the glue of the universe, with several talks on it.

title_en: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Diogenes, 1860
title_el: Ζαν-Λεόν Ζερόμ, Ο Διογένης, 1860
licence: Public domain (Walters Art Museum, 2D work)
why: Athena names Diogenes, with Marcus Aurelius, as proof that freedom is inner (freedom), and tells of the sage who had nothing that Alexander wished to be (myths diogenes, alexander).

title_en: The Great Eleusinian Relief: Demeter, Triptolemos and Persephone, c. 440–430 BC
title_el: Το Μεγάλο Ελευσινιακό Ανάγλυφο: Δήμητρα, Τριπτόλεμος και Περσεφόνη, περ. 440–430 π.Χ.
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer, Gleb Simonov)
why: The Mysteries (mysteries) were Eleusis's; Demeter gives the boy Triptolemos the grain, the seed Athena reads as a programme waiting to grow (myths demeterseed, demeter-seed).

images: Bound legs, bound neck, free hands
title_en: Jan Saenredam after Cornelis van Haarlem, The Cave of Plato, 1604
title_el: Γιαν Σάνρενταμ κατά τον Κορνέλις φαν Χάαρλεμ, Το σπήλαιο του Πλάτωνα, 1604
artist: Jan Saenredam, after Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem
licence: CC0 1.0 (National Gallery of Art Open Access)
why: The Cave (cave) is Athena's favourite allegory, the whole path of awakening in one image; the engraving shows the bound prisoners, the fire and the shadows that myth cave_allegory walks through.

title_en: Hendrick ter Brugghen, Heraclitus, 1628
title_el: Χέντρικ τερ Μπρούγκεν, Ο Ηράκλειτος, 1628
licence: Public domain (Rijksmuseum images are CC0)
why: Heraclitus (heraclitus, weight 5) is for Athena "the most luminous" philosopher, read through the ever-living fire and the child Aion. The painter shows the later "weeping philosopher" type, which is not Athena's reading.

title_en: Aristotle, Roman copy after a bronze by Lysippos
title_el: Ο Αριστοτέλης, ρωμαϊκό αντίγραφο χάλκινου έργου του Λυσίππου
date: Roman copy of an original made after 330 BC
collection: Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Altemps, Rome (Ludovisi Collection, inv. 8575)
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Jastrow: PD-self)
why: Aristotle (aristotle, weight 5) appears in Athena's teaching as Alexander's teacher, who gave him εὖ ζῆν, and as the source of Athena's political anthropology (Nicomachean Ethics and Politics on the bookshelf).

images: Odysseus tied to the mast while fortune's wheel turns
title_en: Siren Painter, Odysseus bound to the mast passes the Sirens, Attic red-figure stamnos, c. 480–470 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος των Σειρήνων, Ο Οδυσσέας δεμένος στο κατάρτι προσπερνά τις Σειρήνες, αττικός ερυθρόμορφος σταμνός, περ. 480–470 π.Χ.
collection: British Museum, London (GR 1843.11-3.31; Cat. Vases E 440)
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Jastrow: PD-self)
why: Athena reads Odysseus asking to be tied to the mast (odysseus-mast; Odyssey 12.160–164 on the bookshelf) as the soul holding its course home to Ithaca (odyssey, ithaca).

images: The desiring part taking the reins of the soul
title_en: The Charioteer of Delphi, bronze, c. 478–474 BC
title_el: Ο Ηνίοχος των Δελφών, χάλκινο άγαλμα, περ. 478–474 π.Χ.
licence: CC0 1.0 (released by the photographer, Jebulon)
why: Athena calls nous the charioteer (ἡνίοχος) of the Phaedrus chariot of the soul (nous, tripartitesoul; myth phaedrus-chariot, Phaedrus 246a on the bookshelf). This is the best-known Greek charioteer, not the winged pair of the myth itself.

title_en: The diver, painted lid of the Tomb of the Diver, Paestum, c. 470 BC
title_el: Ο βουτηχτής, ζωγραφισμένο κάλυμμα του Τάφου του Βουτηχτή, Ποσειδωνία, περ. 470 π.Χ.
licence: CC BY 4.0 (photograph); the painting itself is public domain
attribution: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), via Wikimedia Commons
why: Athena speaks of Diotima's plunge into the open sea (diotima_dive) and of the "Delian diver" one needs to reach Heraclitus. The Paestum diver is the one Greek painting of such a plunge, a funeral image, not an illustration of either.

title_en: Attributed to the Leningrad Painter, Helios, Attic red-figure column krater, c. 480–470 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος του Λένινγκραντ (απόδοση), Ο θεός Ήλιος, αττικός ερυθρόμορφος κιονωτός κρατήρας, περ. 480–470 π.Χ.
licence: CC BY 4.0 (photograph); the vase itself is public domain
attribution: Mark Landon / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
why: The Sun (sun, weight 5) is Plato's image of the Good that Athena unfolds (myths sun-simile, platosun). Helios is the Greek sun god, not Plato's simile itself.

title_en: Persephone Painter, The return of Persephone, with Hermes, Hekate and Demeter, Attic bell-krater, c. 440 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος της Περσεφόνης, Η επιστροφή της Περσεφόνης, με τον Ερμή, την Εκάτη και τη Δήμητρα, αττικός κωδωνόσχημος κρατήρας, περ. 440 π.Χ.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (28.57.23)
licence: CC0 1.0 (Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access)
why: Athena tells how Hermes, guide of souls, leads Persephone back up to Demeter in spring, as the freed go back for the others (myth hermes_persephone_2023; persephone, hermes).

title_en: Pistoxenos Painter, Aphrodite riding a goose, white-ground kylix, c. 460 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος του Πιστόξενου, Η Αφροδίτη πάνω σε χήνα, λευκή κύλικα, περ. 460 π.Χ.
collection: British Museum, London (GR 1869.10-7.77; Cat. Vases D 2)
licence: CC BY 2.5 (photograph); the vase itself is public domain
attribution: Marie-Lan Nguyen / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5/)
why: Athena distinguishes heavenly Aphrodite (Οὐρανία) from common Aphrodite (myth two-aphrodites); here the goddess rides through the air. (The Commons file name says swan; the bird is usually called a goose.)

title_en: Kodros Painter, Aegeus consults Themis on the Delphic tripod, Attic red-figure kylix, 440–430 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος του Κόδρου, Ο Αιγέας ζητά χρησμό από τη Θέμιδα στον δελφικό τρίποδα, αττική ερυθρόμορφη κύλικα, 440–430 π.Χ.
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Bibi Saint-Pol: PD-self)
why: The Delphic oracle on its tripod, painted while it still worked. Athena says mantic knowing is not laurel and tripods (mantike) and tells how the Pythia announced Pythagoras (pythia-announces).

title_en: Painter of London E 497, Orpheus among the Thracians, Attic bell-krater, c. 440 BC
title_el: Ζωγράφος του Λονδίνου Ε 497, Ο Ορφέας ανάμεσα στους Θράκες, αττικός κωδωνόσχημος κρατήρας, περ. 440 π.Χ.
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (24.97.30)
licence: CC0 1.0 (Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access)
why: For Athena, Orpheus (orpheus) is the author of the hymn cycle and the carrier of the flowing light (ΟΡΦΕΑΣ read as ΦΟΡΕΑΣ); the vase shows him singing to the lyre.

images: Athena as the fruiting of Zeus's mind
title_en: Athena springs from the head of Zeus, Attic black-figure amphora, 550–525 BC
title_el: Η Αθηνά γεννιέται από το κεφάλι του Δία, αττικός μελανόμορφος αμφορέας, 550–525 π.Χ.
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Bibi Saint-Pol: PD-self)
why: Athena reads the goddess born from the head of Zeus as wisdom, the fruiting of mind (athenagoddess; myth athena-birth).

title_en: Athena's owl on a silver tetradrachm of Athens, 5th century BC
title_el: Η γλαύκα της Αθηνάς σε ασημένιο αθηναϊκό τετράδραχμο, 5ος αι. π.Χ.
licence: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
why: Athena sets the owl's all-round vision, which turns its head and sees the whole, against the cave prisoner's one-way gaze (athenagoddess, cave).

images: The Parthenon as an 'evolution' of the Acropolis hill
φ in the Acropolis, flowers, shells, the body and galaxies
title_en: Frederic Edwin Church, The Parthenon, 1871
title_el: Φρέντερικ Έντουιν Τσερτς, Ο Παρθενώνας, 1871
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (15.30.67)
licence: CC0 1.0 (Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access)
why: "The Acropolis is my witness": Athena calls the Parthenon an evolution of the hill and finds φ in it (beauty, goldenratio).

title_en: The Ludovisi Ares, Roman copy of a Greek original of c. 320 BC
title_el: Ο Άρης Λουδοβίζι, ρωμαϊκό αντίγραφο ελληνικού πρωτοτύπου του περ. 320 π.Χ.
artist: Unknown; restored by Gian Lorenzo Bernini in 1622
date: Roman copy of an original of c. 320 BC
collection: Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Altemps, Rome (inv. 8602)
licence: Public domain (released by the photographer, Marie-Lan Nguyen as Jastrow: PD-self)
why: Ares (ares, weight 4.5) has a whole talk: Athena reads him as the moment one stands up and acts, and as father, with Aphrodite, of Harmonia and Eros (ares-aphrodite-union).
